lesson.title: Rhythm & Pulse
lesson.complete_text:
You feel the pulse now.

You can count "1, 2, 3, 4" and keep a steady beat. You played an open string on each beat, locked to your body's rhythm.

FOUNDATION COMPLETE - BLOCK 04

Rhythm is the heartbeat. You feel it now.

steps.text:
Imagine someone singing a beautiful melody. Now imagine the same melody with no timing - every note randomly spaced. It falls apart.

Rhythm is what turns notes into music.

Every piece of music has a pulse - a steady beat underneath, like a heartbeat. You can feel it in your chest when you listen to a song you like. Your foot starts tapping.

That tapping? That's rhythm. Your body already knows how to do this.

The pulse is measured in beats. A beat is one steady tap - one unit of time. When you count "1, 2, 3, 4" along with a song, each number is a beat.

The speed of those beats is called tempo.

Music organises beats into bars (also called measures). The most common grouping is 4/4 time - four steady beats in a bar.

"1, 2, 3, 4 - 1, 2, 3, 4 -" That repeating cycle of four is the foundation of most pop, rock, folk, and blues music.

Rhythm isn't just about the beats you play. It's also about the space between notes. A rest (silence) is just as important as a sound.

The gap between notes is where groove lives - where music breathes.

Rhythm isn't a concept. It's a physical thing. You have to feel it in your body before you can play it with your hands.

Do this now - no guitar needed:

1. Stand up or sit straight. Feet flat on the floor.

2. Start tapping your right foot. Steady. Not too fast. Just a comfortable pace.

3. While tapping, count out loud: "1... 2... 3... 4..."

4. Keep going. Feel the pulse in your foot, hear it in your voice. Let them line up.
Now add your hands. Clap on each count. Foot taps, voice counts, hands clap - all on the same beat. This is your body being a rhythm section.
Try this: stop counting out loud, but keep tapping and clapping. Can you feel the "1" without saying it?

choices.label: Yes, the first beat feels heavier

response.text: Right! That heaviness on beat 1 is called the downbeat. It's what gives 4/4 its shape: ONE-two-three-four.

choices.label: Not yet, they all feel the same

response.text: That's normal. Keep tapping. The "1" has a natural weight - it's the beat that feels like "home." Listen for the cycle restarting.

steps.text: Pick up your guitar. We're going to combine rhythm with sound - one note per beat, counting out loud.

Do this:

1. Set a steady foot tap. Count "1, 2, 3, 4" out loud at a comfortable pace.

2. Play the open 6th string (the thickest one) once per beat. Pluck it on each count: 1 - pluck. 2 - pluck. 3 - pluck. 4 - pluck.

3. Keep the foot tapping. Keep counting. Keep the notes even - same length, same space between them.

Notice: you're not playing fast. You're playing steady. Steady is the goal. Speed is irrelevant right now. Evenness is everything.
Did the notes stay even, or did they start bunching up or spreading out?

response.text: Excellent. That's the foundation of rhythm - notes that land exactly on the beat. This is what professional musicians spend their whole lives refining.
That's normal. Stop. Reset. Find the foot tap again. Start over. This is the work - not playing more notes, but playing notes that land exactly on the beat.

steps.text:
You now understand rhythm as the heartbeat of music - the steady pulse that holds everything together. You've felt it in your foot, your hands, your voice.

You know that 4/4 means four steady beats in a bar, with the first beat carrying the weight.

You've played an open string on each beat, keeping time with your body. You know that the space between notes matters - rhythm is as much about silence as sound.

Rhythm is what turns notes into music. Without it, you have sounds. With it, you have a song.
